en: The Śaiśirīya Śikṣā. Hari! Salutations to the illustrious Gaṇapati. May there be no obstacle. Hari! Salutations to the illustrious Gaṇapati. May there be no obstacle.
Salutations to the elephant-faced one, the illustrious lord, the destroyer of all obstacles;
salutations to Viṣṇu in the form of Gaṇeśa, the ten-armed one, whose sole sport is the creation, preservation, and destruction of the universe.
Salutations to that Blessed One, Viṣṇu, who is consciousness and bliss.
Mudgala, Gālava, Gārgya, Śākalya, and likewise Śaiśira—
these five disciples of Śaunaka were the originators of the different recensional branches (śākhā).
And Śaiśira, as well as Śākaṭāyana, having bowed down to the omniscient and omnipotent Teacher, shall proclaim the definition and rule for the branches: "I am Śaiśira; I shall declare the method."
It is held that there are sixty-three or sixty-four phonemes as they occur, whether in Prākṛta or Saṃskṛta; these were proclaimed by the Self-Existent One himself:
twenty-one vowels and twenty-five consonants.
The eight *yādayaḥ* are indeed remembered [as the vowels], while four are remembered as the *yamāḥ*. Likewise, the *anusvāra*, the *visarga*, the *lakāra*,
and what is known as *duḥspṛṣṭa*— these are said to be the nasal (*nāsikya*) range.
Regarding the specific manner of pronunciation, that which depends on the syllables is stated here:
the collection of phonemes is indeed twofold, namely vowels (*svara*) and consonants (*vyañjana*).
Those beginning with *a* are to be known as vowels, while those beginning with *ka* are called consonants.
The vowel (svara) is to be known as twofold: nasal (nāsikya) and resonant (sānunāsika);
likewise, there are the acute (udātta), the grave (anudātta), the circumflex (svarita), and the protracted (pracaya).
Furthermore, the five groups beginning with *ka* are designated as "contacts" (sparśa).

And it should be understood that [the letter] *ḍ* is "lightly touched" (*duḥspṛṣṭa*) when it occurs between vowels; the first letters of the consonant classes (*varga*) and the second letters are designated as "sibilants" (*ūṣman*),
while those excluding the letter *h* are "unvoiced" (*aghoṣa*), and the remainder are called "voiced" (*ghoṣavat*).
The five nasal consonants (*nāsikya*) as well as the *anusvāra* are [nasal];
the four *yamas* are said to be indistinct (*avyakta*) and nasalized (*sānunāsika*).
The four semivowels from *ya* onwards are the *antasthas*, and they too are nasalized, with the exception of *ra*.
The sibilants (ūṣman) and the four beginning with śa are proclaimed [as the fifth group].
The jihvāmūlīya and the upadhmānīya are also mentioned; these two arise from the sibilants and the visarga, depending upon the letter ka.

Vowels are designated by their duration as short (*hrasva*), long (*dīrgha*), or protracted (*pluta*). The duration of the diphthongs (*sandhyakṣara*) is likewise [divided into] long and protracted, and is not merely a single *mātrā*. Here, the distinction is stated with reference to the syllables themselves, based on the specific manner of their pronunciation.
A consonant (vyañjana) shall consist of half a mora (mātrā), and likewise the svarabhakti;

when followed by a conjunct consonant (saṃyoga), the svarabhakti is proclaimed to consist of a quarter-mora (pāda-mātrā). However, an anusvāra following a short vowel is proclaimed to consist of three-quarters of a mora.
That short [vowel] consists of three quarters; these two (the short and long) have equal measures.

However, the anusvāra following a long [vowel] is proclaimed to be one-quarter of a measure; that long [vowel] would thus be one-and-a-quarter [measures]. This is declared to be the duration of a phoneme.

There are eight places of articulation for the phonemes: the chest, the throat, the head, as well as the root of the tongue, the teeth, the nose, the lips, and the palate. The *akuha* sounds (a, k, etc. are said to be produced in the throat; the *upadhmānīya* is produced at the lips.
One should know that *u* and *ū* are labial; likewise, *v* is both dental and labial.
*E* and *ai* are produced by the throat and palate (*kaṇṭhatālavyau*), while *o* and *au* are traditionally held to be produced by the throat and lips (*kaṇṭhoṣṭhajau*).
The manner of articulation (*karaṇa*) for the stops (*sparśas*) is "contact" (*spṛṣṭa*), whereas for the semivowels (*antasthās*) it is said to be "slight."
The articulation of the vowels and the sibilants is traditionally held to be "open" (vivṛta),
while that of the letter *a* is "closed" (saṃvṛta); thus, [the distinction between] all phonemes is explained here based on the specific mode of pronunciation.
In the case of an *anusvāra*, at the end of a pause (*virāma*), and before two syllables,

as well as before the vowels *o* and *ū* and the labial class (*pavarga*), there is a separate [application] for each of these— namely *o*, *au*, and *ū*— in relation to the *anusvāra* and the labial class.
One should separate the two lips during a pause, an opening, and between two consonants; however, for the letter *va*, one should likewise lower the lower lip.
Thus [spoke] Soma, the son of Bhr̥gu, regarding the cows.

"May the excellent praise, which is bliss-bestowing, arise; having flourished, [the hymns] have become peerless. "Tomorrow we shall speak"—such is the illustration regarding the meeting of these vowels—*o*, *au*, *u*, and the consonants.
One should pronounce the eight [vowels] together at once, provided no other vowel intervenes;
"yuyotu" and "yūyuvih" are illustrations of this,
wherein they are always seen in the place of euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*).
One should indeed cause the hero to be employed there by his own group; "Hing-kṛṇvatī," "Tatte bhadram," and "Gāṃ bhajanta nidarśanam" [are the mantras].
When joined with the fifth of the *sparśa* consonants, they are traditionally known here as the *yamās*.

That which is equal to an iron ball is proclaimed as having dense bonds; "that [fire] seized the aged women, the fire seized the sacrifice, the wife seized the husband"— this is the illustration for "we have seized the self, we have grasped it."

Likewise, the *sparśa* consonants excluding the fifth class, when joined with the semivowels (*antaḥstha*), are proclaimed to have loose bonds, being similar to a block of wood; [in such cases], one might encounter an enemy, supreme friendship, or hardship—where is the thunderbolt? The sacrificer prospers in the kingdom.
The examples are "plāyogi," "viddhi," "meḍhraṃ," and "vādhyam.
When the letter *va* is joined with the letters *na* or *ṇa*,
it is to be known as having a loose articulation (*ślathabandha*), and in this context, it is called "duḥspṛṣṭa" (imperfectly contacted).
"I praise Bhūridāvna, Evayāvan, and Dadhikrāvan who comes at dawn;
I praise Heaven and Earth. In this context, however, the illustration is:
"The steed [is praised]," where *ś*, *ṣ*, and *s* are preceded by a consonant and followed by a nasalized vowel (*anunāsika*).
If there were a mutual conjunction of the tangibles, they would be proclaimed as having loose bonds, like a mass of wool; "May Viṣṇu, the smearer of ghee, pervade [them]," is the illustration.
There is no audible [separation] for that which precedes it, nor for a consonant at the pause; for example:
*vāgdevīviṭ* from *kulāt*, *vibhrāḍ bṛhad āre* from *panthām*, *yad ghnann triṣṭub gāyatrī*, and *asmād anuṣṭub*. These are the illustrations.
When a word ending in the letter *na* is followed by a word beginning with the letter *ya*,
it should be understood as uncombined (*asaṃyuta*); however, the manifestation of both [sounds] is desired if the two *ya*s are combined and the vowel *ṛ* follows.
In this context, however, a conjunct consonant (*saṃyuta*) is to be understood; the manifestation of both [consonants] is not intended.
But when a *anusvāra*, a vowel, and so forth precede a conjunct, it is pronounced twice.
If a sibilant (*ūṣman*) follows, the first two are to be known as such; likewise, after the letter *l*, a contact consonant (*sparśa*) followed by *r* is treated similarly.
Mount the chariot of faith for our well-being; mount the foremost chariot of the thunderbolt.
O thou who art strengthened by might, draw near with thy vast powers.
Who stands behind the meters? Who is the one who shoots the arrows that are well-sung? Who is the one who hurls them?

Like a bright torch falling from heaven, it shines with a flowing luster; it increases the ancient light that was previously hidden. And here is the illustration of this: if the heat is joined with a suffix ending in *y*, then its movement [of substitution] must be performed; "śyāvāḥ svāhā," I invoke for the sake of prosperity.
When the two letters *na* and *ṭa* occur together with a following *sa*, a *ta* arises between them;
for those two [nasals], there is a homogeneous letter in the *ca*-group (*cavarga*), but for the subsequent [consonant], it is indeed *ta*.
Furthermore, in the words *aduka*, *heman*, *vṛtta*, and *ākāra*, the vowel *a* is heard.

O Waters, you are praised as one who possesses [all things]—as the Virāj and Samrāj—in whom men are born and from whom this world is perceived; this is the illustration. And whatever sound is emitted, characterized by its first utterance, [is likewise praised]. The waters [are thus addressed]. This is the demonstration.
When the first letters, which are infinite in number, stand before a sound known as *ghoṣa*,
they are called the second letters by those who know phonetics;
in both cases, the vowel *ā* is heard as if it were a wooden shoe or gold.
The waters [responded] with the sound produced by the second utterance,
"vṛkṣe vṛkṣe saṃvatsaraṃ tvānthsāri tamapsanta camasaraḥ matsyapāyī";
this indeed is the illustration.
Just as that rutting elephant steps from foot to foot,
so too should each syllable be made distinct at the end of its preceding one,
where *r* and *l* follow a vowel when a sibilant (*ūṣman*) stands next.
The *svarabhakti* (vowel-fragment) is declared to be possible after a preceding vowel; for example:
*adarśi śīrṣā agniḥ*, *hotā sarsṛte ca na*, *jalhavaḥ śatavalśo'rṣā*, and *ṇo'rṣan*—these are the illustrations here.
When joined with consonants at the end [of a word], that same [vowel] shall be the measure of the foot;
as it spreads from head to head, this is the illustration for one employing *svarabhakti*, who should avoid three faults.
The vowel *i*, the vowel *u*, likewise the fault of being swallowed (*grasta*),
and the letters *ya* and *ra* joined with the letter *v*— in these cases, the lips do not quiver; this is quickly proclaimed [as the rule].
"pra kṛtāny ṛjīṣiṇaḥ," "vajrī ṛcīṣamaḥ," "śamy ṛkvāṇaḥ," "niḥ ṛthan," and "niḥ ṛteś cāpi nidarśanam"— in such cases as these,
when the *visarjanīya* occurs before two *ka* sounds (*kapaḥ*).
There is no *saṃhitā* (euphonic combination) when the two [words] are produced from a sibilant (*ūṣman*) and are included [in the following rule],
as in *jyotiṣkṛd yātam*, *chardiṣpāvimam*, and *añjas pāmu*; however, the examples are found in *ubhaye haviṣkṛtam* and *pathas pathaḥ*.

A low-pitched tone is the *anudātta* (unaccented), while a high-pitched one is called the *udātta* (accented). The combination of these two is the *svarita* (circumflex); their unification is known as *pracaya* (the continuous accent).
The *anudātta* is to be understood as residing in the heart, while the *udātta* is said to be in the head.
The *svarita* [accent] is located at the root of the ear, while the *pracaya* occurs throughout the entire [syllable];
"imaṃ me gaṅge yamune sarasvati" is an illustration of this;
likewise, there are the *udātta*, the *anudātta*, and the *svarita*.
I shall describe the characteristics, the deity, and the vehicle itself: one should know that white is high-pitched, while red is said to be low;
one should know that dark (śyāma) is modulated (svarita); and Agni is the deity of the high-pitched tone.
One should know that the low tone (nīca) is Soma; likewise, the circumflex (svarita) is Savitṛ.
One should know the acute (udātta) as Brāhmaṇa, while the low tone is said to be Kṣatriya;
one should know the circumflex as Vaiśya, and the acute as Bharadvāja.

They say that the *gautama* [meter] is low-pitched (*nīca*), while they know the *gārgya* to be circumflex (*svarita*). One should know the *gāyatra* to be acute (*udātta*), the *traiṣṭubha* is said to be low-pitched, and one should know the *jāgata* to be circumflex; this is the fixed rule.
In the middle, however, one should perform the *kaṃpa* (tremor); both sides should be equal. The *pāda-kaṃpa* is intended to be twice the duration of the vowel (*varṇakāla*).
Having taken up the *anudātta* (low-pitched), one should indeed support the *svarita* (circumflex).
If it should return after being struck down, this is known as the procedure for shaking (*kaṃpa*);
"Where are the horses being yoked by us? O Indra, you are indeed [powerful]"—this is the illustration.
One should shake the shaking (*kampa*) like a charioteer; this is the illustration.
When the preceding portion is acute (udātta) and the following portion is depressed (nihanyate),
it is called an "acute-circumflex" (udāttakampa); this is also observed in certain instances,
such as *śacī3pati* and *tanū3napāt*, which serve as illustrations based on their positions.
At the time of reciting the *krama*, one should not shake the *ratha* [text] as one does the *saṃhitā*;
here, only the low (*nīca*) and acute (*svarita*) tones are prescribed—this is remembered as the rule for shaking.
A wise person, established in self, tranquil, and fearless, should pronounce the phonemes.
One should not strike [the tongue] against [the palate], nor should one strike it away; one should neither sing [the vowels] nor cause them to tremble.
Just as one should pronounce the phonemes, so too should one bring them to completion, fixing the gaze on the tip of the hand while reflecting upon the meaning of the scripture.
One should pronounce the syllables equally with both the hand and the mouth;
for the voice and the hand together constitute a pair.
One who falters from the hand or falters from the voice does not enjoy the fruit of the Veda.
One who is not deformed, nor has protruding lips, nor is indistinct, nor nasalized, nor stammers, nor has a bound tongue, is able to speak the phonemes;
he whose nature is auspicious and whose teeth and lips are beautiful.
One who is both bold and humble is fit to speak the syllables;
just as a tigress carries her cubs by her teeth yet does not wound them—
fearing both their falling and their being torn— one should employ the syllables in that same manner.
The *saṃhitā* brings forth the sun; the *pada*s bring forth the station of the moon;
the *krama* leads to the sun, which is the effort toward the healthy state.
But he who studies [the Veda] devoid of the hands [of proper recitation], lacking vowels and phonemes, [attains nothing].
One who has been consumed by the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāman [is purified and] enters a superior womb; and one who recites them with his hand [properly] applies the accents and phonemes.
Purified by the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāman, he attains the world of Brahmā.
As is the voice, so are the hands; one should avoid them being empty.
Wherever the voice is situated, there the hands remain as well.
Niṣāda and Gāndhāra are high, while Ṛṣabha and Dhaivata are low.
The remaining notes—Ṣaḍja, Madhyama, and Pañcama—are to be known as svarita (circumflex).
The bull (the hand) indicates the udātta (acute) when its head is placed at the base of the forefinger;
it indicates the svarita when held at the end and in the middle [of the forefinger]; and it indicates the anudātta (grave) when held at the little finger.

Like lightning in the sky, like a thread through a crystal or a gem, such is the severance of the revolutions for one who is discerning of the measures; the half-measure follows the measure, and thus it conforms to the measure.
The *pākavatī* [verse] has short syllables at both ends and long syllables in the middle; the *pipīlikā* [meter] is likewise.
"One [god] has come hither today with his chariot having a golden front-board"—this [verse], addressed to the Ādityas who uphold the sacred law (*dhṛtavratāḥ*), is an illustration of that.
One employing *svarabhakti* should avoid three faults:
the sound *ikāra*, the sound *ukāra*, and likewise the fault of being swallowed (*grasta*).
It should not be pronounced in the former part of the vowel, nor in the latter part, under any circumstances.
Neither in the vowel nor in the mora [is the distinction made]; how then is the *svāra* accent prescribed?

When that which belongs to the subsequent member occurs before [the junction], and that which belongs to the preceding member occurs after it—in the conjunction of these two halves of the halves—the wise one should apply the *svāra* accent.
Just as a powerful king might seize the kingdom of one who is weak,
so too does a strong vowel carry away a weak consonant;
whether it be a syllable of one mora or two morae, if it is here pronounced with a vowel, [the consonant is subordinated].
Its final portion consists of half a mora, and likewise there is an excess of one mora;
moreover, the *obhāva*, the *vivṛtti*, the sibilants *śa*, *ṣa*, and *sa*, the *repha*,
the *jihvāmūlīya*, and the *upadhmānīya*— this is the eightfold path of the *uṣman*.
If there is a connection between both [vowels and consonants], one should know that the supreme state beginning with *u* and ending in a vowel is of such a nature;
whatever else exists, distinct from the sibilants (*ūṣman*),
consists of vowels, tremors, and phonemes (*raṅga*), which possess their own durations by their very nature.
When they are being recited by a speaker who employs rapid effort, they increase [in length].
The letter *ya* is said to be of three kinds: heavy (*guru*), light (*laghu*), and lightest (*laghūtara*).
It is heavy at the beginning [of a word], light in the middle, and lightest at the end of a word.

It should be understood that the sound *ja* occurs at the beginning of a word, at the beginning of a foot (*pāda*), and in the case of conjunct consonants (*saṃyoga*) and *avagrahas*; elsewhere it is traditionally known as *ya*.
Furthermore, this single syllable is treated like the end of a word (*padānta*).
It should possess sweetness yet not be indistinct; it should be clear yet not mumbled.
Just as in a well-governed land the castes do not intermingle, so too [the recitation] should be free from confusion.
One who sings, one who recites too fast, one who shakes his head, and likewise one who merely reads from a written text [are to be avoided].
One who does not understand the meaning, one with a weak voice— these six are the lowest of reciters.
Sweetness, clarity of syllables, clarity of words, a melodious tone, composure, and being joined with lightness— these six are the qualities of a reciter.
The first [consonant] should be known as *rākṣa* (*ra*), and the other (*kha*) would be *khna*;
there the *yamās* turn back like kinsmen from a cremation ground when the first and last members of a class are joined with the final member of that same class.
Having pronounced the nasalized guru [consonant], one should speak of that which resides in the station of *Yama*;
the resonance (*nāda*) is heard from the sound, from the pause, and likewise from the doubling [of the consonant]. Thus, what was previously non-nasal becomes nasalized by way of its phonetic form.
Dadhyañ indeed displayed his heroic power in the highest heaven; this is the illustration.

The substitution of *r* for a final *n* before a vowel is prescribed, but there is elision (*lopa*) when it is preceded by *ā*; however, when *s* or *ś* follows those two [sounds], they remain as they are.
O friends, win over the bridegroom;
he will delight every limb joined with the nasal sound (*nāsikya*),
just as water colored with lac delights one whose limbs and voice are marked by the letter *na*.
One should understand all musical tones (*raṅga*) as being like kinsmen; the tone arising from the heart is like well-tuned bell-metal,
possessing both one-mora (*mātrika*) and two-mora (*dvimātra*) durations, as illustrated by the word *jaghanbām*.

Just as a woman from Saurāṣṭra is called "takrām," so should the vowels (*raṅga*) be applied in the *kha* [vowel] as if in the *ara*. When the letter *na* has been elided by the *śvedayā* [process], Śaunaka and others color the vowel with that [following] vowel.
This is declared to be the "beginning of all musical notes" (ādisarvaraṅga), but do not fear it. I shall now proclaim to you the seven musical notes (svaras) and their very characteristics:
the jātya, the kṣaipra, the abhinihita, and the tairovyañjana.
A vowel of the same class [is called] *sajātya*; O Agni, when it is heard with readiness, it is called *kṣaipra*.
They increased: the *abhinihita* and the *tairovyañjana* for the sake of aid;
the *tirovirāma* is when [the pause] is held apart, and the *praśliṣṭa* is as in "O Indra, lover of songs."
Who knows *pādavṛtta*, *kari*, the seven *svaras*, and so forth?
The three *svaras* beginning with *jāti* and ending with *pādavṛtta* are the *svaritas*;
that which is high (*udātta*) in the preceding junction and situated low (*nīcais*) upon the word is [the *svarita*].
The remaining [vowel] following an unraised (anudātta) tone is prescribed by Śākala and others as having the raised (udātta) sound heard in its place of modulation for half a mora;
however, in the case of artificial [recitation], it varies in many ways at the junction of word-endings and beginnings in the Ṛgveda verses.

However, in the *Ṛgveda*, thirty phonemes— distinguished by elision (*lopa*), augmentation (*āgama*), modification (*vikāra*), and so forth, and categorized as *sparśas*, *antasthas*, and *ūṣmans*— are traditionally taught in sequence by the teachers as being useful for euphonic combination (*saṃyoga*).
The three [worlds] in the three realms, whatever is heard above, the intermediate space, and that which pertains to the soil— this is characterized by being unfolded;
it is the one who rests outside, the one seen separately, the seer, the bull, the great one in the three.
This is the characteristic of the closed [vowels] for the duration of a year;
however, regarding the contact of consonants with consonants, whatever mutual conjunction may occur,
the retention of the preceding [consonant] in the mouth is not intended by the Śruti.
If a conjunction of consonants were to occur with one another, there would be no hearing of the preceding [vowel] at the pause of a consonant; for instance,
in the case of *kakudmān* and *yad ghnann bhinadmi*, there is the preservation of the individual phonemes (*dārṇasya sandhṛtiḥ*).

Agni holds the grey-haired women like a hunter; the syllables *ga*, *ka*, and *gha* belong to Vāgdevī, purified by speech, from the clan of the Viś; Vibhrāj, Bṛhat, Āraik, Panthām, Yaddhnan, Triṣṭubh, Gāyatrī, Arvāk, and Ṣal—these follow after the Anuṣṭubh.
The illustration is that there are four contacts, not five; for if such contacts were possible,
then in the case of the fifth [note], the third of itself would be reached, and likewise the fifth [of the fifth].

When a letter at the end of a word belongs to a consonant class (varga), it takes the third letter of its own class when followed by the third or fourth letters of another class, as well as when joined with semivowels (antasthā); furthermore,
the first letter of each class [takes the third] when followed by a fifth letter of any class.
In the *udaya* (rising) of the fifth [syllable], there shall not be the letter *ca* at the end of a word: *arvāgdevā*, *vibhrāḍbṛhat*, *bṛhadbhirvājais*, *triṣṭubbhis*, *arvāgratham*,
*samrāḍvibhvīs*, *gomat*, and *yūyamudrebham*.
"May the bull come hither, O Mitra and Varuṇa;
may he turn back from the three-peaked mountain"—this is also an illustration here.
Furthermore, when a *ha* follows a word-final consonant belonging to a class of sounds (*varga*), [it undergoes elision].
One should reach that which is the fourth of the first [group], namely the letter *ha*; and having reached that fourth, one reaches the first *ha*,
for it thus attains its own third [position] as the preceding syllable.

In *ṛdhak*, *dhruvam*, *samrāṭ*, *ḍhaṃtā*, *kaddhanūnām*, and those formed with *triṣṭubh*, the letter *k* does not occur at the end of a word; therefore, it is not taught [as a final consonant]. Furthermore, when a final *m* is followed by *r* or a sibilant (*ūṣman*), [the rules for its modification apply].
The *anusvāra* occurs even when [the vowels] are situated in the middle of a word:
*tvaṃ rathaṃ*, *taṃ hinvanti*, *tvaṃ śukrasya*, *tāṃ su te kīrtim*, *samānodayodarkam*, *ṣaṣṭhe'hani*, *māṃsamekaḥ piṃśati*, *cakṣūṃṣi*, *maṃhiṣṭhaḥ*.

In this regard, my own example here is as follows: among the consonants, specifically in the case of the semivowels (*antasthā*) and the objects of touch (*sparśa*), it is traditionally taught that those very [semivowels] are the substitutes for the letter *m*. Furthermore, when followed by the fifth letter of its own class, the same rule applies.

This letter *m* at the end of a word, when preceded by a stop (*sparśa*), becomes homogeneous with the following sound; however, in all cases, it remains nasalized (*anunāsika*). This [rule] applies in the verse of the poet: "I bow to Him with these words; no one strikes Him."
He who made this, knowing it—those gods, that cow;
may you be auspicious in the filter. O Bṛhaspati, [grant] that desirable fortune which is within the intermediate and outer [worlds]; thus [is] the nasalized [syllable] situated within.
That which one attains without the letter *repha* is indeed that which is supreme beyond this;
"this world is the end of the yoke" is the illustration.
Even the letter *na* [is treated] as the letter *la*, and that letter *la* is nasalized (*sānunāsika*).
The illustration for this is found in the passage "yo jigīvāṃ lakṣam ādadat.
In that case, the letter *t* at the end of the word becomes *l* before both *l* and *j*,
as seen in "aṅgād-aṅgāl-lomno-lomnaḥ" and "yaj-jātavedaḥ."

When the *ṅa* and *na* at the end of a word are followed by the letter *ha* or *ṣa* within the same word, they become pure *ha* and *ṣa*. Then one should state that the pure *ṛ* and *ā* [are treated as follows]:
*dadhy-aṅ*, *hārv-āṅ*, *havāmahe devān*, *huvema*, *mahān hy asya*.
Regarding the example "vātān hyaśvān dan ṣalakṣam," wherever a *ha* with a preceding *na* is perceived,
one should first pronounce the sound of the *na* and then join it with the *ha*.
Wherever the letter *ṣ* is seen following the letter *n*,
one should pronounce the *n* and then join it with the *ṣ*; furthermore,
when the letter *h* follows, the preceding word ending in *ṅ* [is joined accordingly].
Having performed the hearing of the syllable *ṅa*, one should again join it with the syllable *ha*.
However, in artificial [Vedic] texts, at the junctions of word-endings and beginnings, it is divided in many ways within the *ṛc*s;
specifically, according to the sequence in the *ṛc*, there are elisions, augmentations, modifications, and so forth.

In this regard, thirty phonemes are traditionally enumerated by the teachers of the Ṛgveda as subsisting upon conjunctions, distinguished by the categories of *sparśa* (stops), *antastha* (semivowels), and *ūṣman* (sibilants and aspirates);
[the rule applies] when a word beginning with *sa-* follows one ending in *ṭa*, *na*, or *sa*.
In that interval, they may likewise be *virāṭ* and *samrāṭ*; when *sasavan* occurs before *cañajeṣu*, the letter *ñ* arises in place of the letter *n*.
O Mitra, drive away those who have grown arrogant; O hero, slay the enemies, O Jāmi.
If a word ending in *ṅa* precedes and one beginning with *sa* follows, and the letter *ka* occurs between them, it is *pratyak*; for example, as in *viśve*.
However, if *ṅa* and *śa* are at the ends of two words and the letter *ka* occurs between them, [the same applies].

If a word beginning with *ś* follows a word ending in one of the first letters of a varga (*c*, *t*, *t*, *k*), it undergoes *chatva* (the substitution of *ch*) as if it were a separate entity; for example, *arvāṅkśaśvat-tamam* becomes *arvāṅkśaśva-c-chat-tamam*, just as *tacchaṃyoḥ* becomes *tacchaṃyoḥ*. Similarly, the *ś* in *śaphau* becomes *ch* when preceded by *arvāk*.

Regarding the statement "The *vipāṭ* and *śutudrī* [verses] are examples for the remainder of the *triṣṭubh*," this refers to a case where a word ending in *n* is followed by one beginning with *ś*; if that *n* becomes *ñ*, there must be a *c* between them.
"ghaneva vajrīñchannathi hyamitrān"— this is the illustration.
When a *visarga* at the end of a word occurs before *ś*, *ṣ*, or *s*,
it then undergoes doubling (*dvitva*) and its original form (*prakṛti*) is also prescribed.
When the two letters *ka* and *kha* follow it, a sibilant (*ūṣman*) may occur;
those consonants (*sparśa*) which are gutturals (*kaṇṭhya*) combined with vowels (*svara*) are then formed into clusters (*piṇḍakṛta*).
Listen now to this illustration for all of them, as previously described.
Just as drivers bind grass by wrapping it with a thong, so too is the Vedic *piṇḍa* said to be wrapped with the syllable *ya*:
"O you who are well-disposed toward Vadhryaśva, O friends of Vadhryaśva, [grant] prosperity."
Tryambaka, Kṛtānī, Ṛjīṣin,
Sadhryañc, Ṛtū, Taugrya, Vajrin, Acīṣama, Eṣṭṛ, Ṛkvā, Ādrvanna, Aśatru, Arya, Uṣas, and Ṛṣikṛt.
The two *mṛ* sounds produced at the tip of the tongue, joined together and pronounced as one without a hiatus, rounded like a wick—
may the Ṛṣis of the quarters, through the Nirṛti-rite, attend upon Nirṛti and Nirṛtha.

Agni, whose power is manifest, has been praised with songs by the ancient seers; O Lord of Seasons, you who are the seasons themselves, being exhilarated, you strike down those of evil intent; our thoughts are exhilarated, the wives of the heart are exhilarated, and light is the illuminator of the heart.
The letter *ha*, joined with the fifth [consonants] and combined with the semivowels (*antasthā*), should be pronounced from the chest;
thus do the Bahvṛcas desire it. "I invoke Hradunī, Agni, O Hlādikā, O Hlādikāvatī."
For his greatness is demonstrated by the expression "Brahman-Brahma" (brahmabrahmā);

[his nature consists of] place, time, and modification; the concealed and the revealed grammatical traditions; slight contact, lack of voiced articulation, vowel quality, tremor, and likewise the quality of aspiration.
The deities are the phonemes, both nasalized and non-nasalized; however,
the wise declare that the *praṇava* consists of four morae and six morae, according to as many properties as exist in each respective case.
The former is the vowel (svara), the latter is the resonance (nāda); they are proclaimed to have equal measure.
The vowel is to be known as the *anudātta* (unraised tone), while the resonance is called the *udātta* (raised tone).
This is the definition of the *praṇava*; the *praṇava* is celebrated as Brahman.
He who knows that which is like an unbroken stream of oil, possessing the resonance of a long bell, which is the downward-born tip of the *praṇava*— he is a knower of the Veda;
it has three stations, three measures, is the triple Brahman, and consists of three syllables.
He who knows that which consists of three moras and half a mora is a knower of the Veda;
for the Veda is a collection of phonemes, and the Veda is celebrated as Brahman.
Therefore, he who knows those phonemes of the Veda is honored in the world of Brahman.
Chandas is his feet, Jyotiṣa his pair of eyes, Kalpa his hands, Nirukta his pair of ears,
Śikṣā his nose, and Vyākaraṇa his mouth.
Salutations be to this Viṣṇu, the soul of the Vedas;
to Viṣṇu, the primordial god whose limbs are the six parts and the senses, the soul of the Vedas, the Puruṣa of universal form.
The twice-born who recites this hymn to the God with full reflection goes to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu; *Oṃ*.
Thus ends the Śaiśirīya Śikṣā.
